articles.title: South Korea recalls Ukraine envoy over prisoner-of-war row
articles.summary: It is the latest in a diplomatic spat after Kyiv disclosed that two North Korean prisoners were transferred to Seoul.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images By Yvette Tan 
- Published 8 October 2026 
South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the latest escalation in a diplomatic spat between both countries. 
It started last month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul. 
Seoul says Ukraine broke an agreement to keep the transfer a secret but Zelensky's office maintains that there was no non-disclosure agreement in place. 
The two North Korean soldiers, who were among thousands from the country supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea. 
South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo had in September lodged a formal complaint with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Vieshkin over the matter. 
And earlier this week, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said he received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, but added that it fell short of Seoul's expectations, according to local reports. 
Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said in a statement on Thursday that "diplomacy should prevail over emotions". 
"Despite Seoul's decision to recall its ambassador, Ukraine remains open to restoring a constructive dialogue - even if it takes time," he said. 
Earlier on Thursday, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said in a statement it would "continue consultations with the Ukrainian side", adding that it expected that "various outstanding issues...[would] be resolved smoothly".

- Published 11 January 2025 
-

- Published 7 May 
Zelensky had revealed the transfer at a speech at the UN General Assembly in September, adding that the two North Koreans had not been "easy to capture alive". 
It prompted a swift condemnation from South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who called it "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security. 
President Lee also faced heavy criticism at home in light of the revelation, with local opposition accusing him of wanting to cover up the transfer to appease Pyongyang. 
But his office said that it had been kept confidential partly to protect the North Koreans' families and added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war. 
Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer. 
The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement. 
Seoul later demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations. 
Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war. 
After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks. 
This July, Seoul had announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment. 
Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take. 
South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US. 
Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.

articles.title: Many Nepalis swept away in the floods aren't officially dead, leaving families in limbo
articles.summary: Relatives are finding themselves with no compensation and facing an administrative nightmare.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
In Hindu tradition, when a body cannot be recovered, a symbolic effigy is made from sacred "kusha" grass to represent the dead By Azadeh Moshiri South Asia correspondent 
- Published 6 October 2026 
At the Pashupatinath temple, on the banks of the Bagmati River in Kathmandu, Madan Lal Lawat joined other families in honouring loved ones who were lost when a deadly flood tore through the China-Nepal border last month. 
In Hindu tradition, when a body cannot be recovered, a symbolic effigy is made from sacred "kusha" grass to represent the dead, allowing relatives to perform last rites. 
With more than 5,000 people still missing and the government ending rescue operations, this is the only way people like Lawat can honour the dead. 
Five of his relatives - including his brother - were caught in the water's onslaught and are still missing. Lawat survived because he was driving his bus outside his village, Betrawati. 
The last Lawat heard from survivors is that his brother Mangal died while going door-to-door, trying to warn others to leave. 
"I don't know how to start over. Police say they're still searching for the bodies, but I'm not sure they'll ever be found," Lawat says. 
He has little doubt they are dead. 
But legally, their fate is far more complicated. In Nepal, a missing person is only presumed dead after 12 years. 
Image source, Supplied Image caption, 
The last Madan Lal Lawat heard from survivors is that his brother Mangal (pictured) died while going door-to-door, trying to warn others to leave 
Section 40 of Nepal's Civil Code does allow for some exceptions, but it does not have a provision for disasters like the flood witnessed last month. 
Families like Lawat's have told the BBC they are struggling to obtain death certificates, affecting everything from accessing flood compensation to the transfer of properties and even inheritance. 
Relatives can receive up to 25,000 rupees (£122; $162) for funeral costs, in addition to about 200,000 rupees (£981; $1,302) in bereavement compensation for the first relative who died, and 100,000 rupees (£491; $651) for each additional death. 
But this is only possible once they submit a death certificate. So as families try to rebuild their lives, many are now caught in an administrative nightmare. 
"In view of the current disaster, the law is outdated," says constitutional law expert, Bipin Adhikari. 
He explains the law was meant to account for people who travelled abroad and weren't heard from for years. "But technology has advanced now, it isn't as difficult to send or receive information," he argues. 
For Lawat, the legal minefield has made an already devastating loss even harder to navigate. 
When he tried to obtain a death certificate last week, officials at the local municipality office turned him away. "They said they're still discussing the death certificate issue. We aren't sure what to do now. There's so much uncertainty," he tells us. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Most of Betrawati village was swallowed up in the floods 
Even when bodies are recovered, identifying their identities is a slow and challenging task. More than 1,400 bodies have been recovered so far, and Nepal has little experience in processing DNA at such scale. In some cases, authorities have taken DNA samples, then buried the bodies with markers in the ground, should families claim them. 
Given the scale of damage and loss, families say compensation is desperately needed. 
Nepal's latest assessment counts 7,570 private buildings damaged or destroyed, home to nearly 33,000 people based on census data. 
The BBC visited Lawat's village Betrawati just days after the disaster, once the roads to the district of Rasuwa had been cleared. For days, this area had been cut off from the capital Kathmandu, and struggling with a shortage of basic supplies including petrol. 
The damage in the village was staggering. The ground was nothing but hardened mud and silt. Footage of the flood showed it had swallowed most of the village in just minutes. There was no sign of its bustling market, the local Uttargaya School was in ruins, the houses swept away, and school buses were turned over. 
Betrawati straddles flood-devastated Rasuwa and Nuwakot, and is part of the Bidur municipality, where the government estimates more than 3,000 buildings have been damaged or destroyed. It's the largest amount of any municipality. 
Local governments are now urging the prime minister's office to figure out a way to resolve the death confirmation issue. 
"Everything is on hold," Bidur's Mayor, Rajan Shrestha, told the BBC. 
He said it could take up to 12 years for relatives to access the funds they are entitled to. 
For one of South Asia's smallest economies, finding money for compensation is a challenge, and the sums on offer are small when compared with the scale of the losses. 
Image source, Supplied Image caption, 
More than 5,000 people are still missing after the floods, leaving families stricken with grief 
The government puts damage to personal belongings alone at £123 million ($165 million) across more than 8,300 households. 
This implies losses of about £14,800 ($20,000) on average per household, though this figure is only based on census data and modelling, and doesn't represent the exact cost per family. 
The financial toll makes the death certificates vital for families trying to recover from the disaster. 
Shrestha is calling on the federal government to resolve the issue as soon as possible. Until then, he says his hands are tied. 
"We understand the emotional pain for families who have already performed funeral rituals, but officials must work within legal boundaries to avoid future liabilities." 
The government has told the BBC it is trying to find a solution. 
In a statement, the prime minister's office said it was "aware of the difficulties" the law may cause families in "exceptional circumstances, including disasters". The home ministry said the government was taking the issue seriously and was ready to amend the law, if required. 
The legal hurdles families are facing comes as Nepal faces a steep reconstruction bill, which the government says could cost up to £3.6bn ($4.8bn). 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Relatives carry Kush grass effigies for cremation during symbolic funerals held for flood victims still reported missing 
At the UN General Assembly in New York, Prime Minister Balen Shah explained rebuilding the country would require more than 10% of its gross domestic product, an enormous burden on the country's economy. 
Dozens of public buildings including schools, health clinics and hospitals have been wrecked by the floods. That's in addition to roads, bridges, wastewater treatment plants and hydropower projects. 
Shah is now pushing for grant-based international support rather than new loans. Nepal is one of the lowest emitters of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet one one of the most vulnerable countries to global warming. 
"When a climate-driven disaster destroys infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan or a patchwork of small grants," he told a room full of world leaders. 
This is not the first time Nepal has had to recover after a devastating natural disaster. 
For Tisum Ghale, the past month has been painfully familiar. 
He and his family lost their home in an earthquake in 2015, and became displaced for months. They eventually settled in Betrawati. 
But the place that was once a refuge is where 19 of his relatives were killed in last month's flood, including five of his sisters. He survived because he was doing construction work outside of the village. 
Once again, he is without a home. 
"I have lost everything," he said. 
So far he has received no compensation. He desperately needs the money after his home was washed away and he looks after eight children left behind by his sisters. He is one of the thousands displaced, living across 37 holding centres in northern Nepal. 
Like Lawati and thousands of other families, Ghale plans on holding a funeral without his loved ones' bodies. 
He hopes the law will eventually recognise what he already knows: his loved ones will not be coming home.

articles.title: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'
articles.summary: Several member states of the international tribunal, including the UK, say they "strongly disagree" with the sanctions.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
The ICC said it would not be "deterred" by the sanctions By Tom Bateman ,  State department correspondent ,  Anna Holligan ,  Reporting from in The Hague,   and   Florence Freeman 
- Published 9 October 2026 
The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution. 
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans. 
The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order. 
The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. 
The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially. 
However, the US has provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns. 
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar". 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Marco Rubio said that "either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC" 
The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support" for the ICC and said they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions. 
They also praised the court's staff for their work bringing "those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice", as well as supporting victims. 
The ICC was founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and counts 125 countries as member states. Several major countries remain outside the ICC, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel. 
The Trump administration argues the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty. 
It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted. 
But Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC." 
The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software. 
Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution. 
He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories, including the UK, to "rein in" the institution. 
The Netherlands, which hosts the court in The Hague and is also a Nato ally of the US, faces particular pressure. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has said the sanctions would seriously affect the court's ability to function. 
Netanyahu welcomed the sanctions, saying the ICC was "not a court" but a political body that threatened law-abiding democracies and "the very idea of national sovereignty". 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Among those awaiting trial in The Hague is Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines 
The ICC said that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting its work and intimidating those who co-operate with it - but that it "will not be deterred". 
It called the measures "an assault on the rule of law" and said no one should be punished for serving the cause of justice, adding: "History will judge this moment." 
This showdown potentially marks the gravest crisis in the court's 24-year history. Rather than targeting individual ICC judges and prosecutors, the US is now sanctioning the court itself. 
The sanctions could ultimately see the ICC unable to try cases, meaning detainees awaiting trial or judgment could have to be released, according to Professor Ryan Goodman from the New York University School of Law. 
Among those awaiting trial in The Hague is Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines. 
The 81-year-old is accused of the extrajudicial killing of thousands during his deadly "war on drugs" between 2011 and 2019. Others awaiting trial or with pending appeals include former senior figures accused of war crimes in Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic. 
Goodman says that as a senator, Rubio was "out front" highlighting Duterte's alleged crimes. 
He told the BBC such a release would be "enormously damaging to the global effort towards international justice [and] towards the Philippines". 
"[For] the victims, it just has to be incredibly traumatic because a lot of them participate in the ICC proceedings to put themselves on the line with a hope that justice will come around," adds Goodman, a former special counsel at the US Department of Defence. 
Among the carve-outs announced as part of today's sanctions are "licenses" allowing the ICC to continue "services for the operation of facilities used for the detention" of Duterte and others. 
However, Goodman says ultimately these detainees may have to be released "as a matter of law" if the financial sanctions mean the court cannot conduct fair trials or appeals.

articles.title: JD Vance casts doubt on firing squad execution and says he will not watch it
articles.summary: The planned execution of Nidal Hasan by firing squad would be the first military execution in more than 60 years.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
"I'm not going to be watching it" - JD Vance on possible livestreamed execution By Nardine Saad   and   Kali Hays 
- Published 9 October 2026 
US Vice-President JD Vance has cast doubt on the Pentagon's plans to livestream a firing squad execution of the Fort Hood attacker. 
Vance expressed uncertainty to reporters about whether the December execution would go ahead as planned, saying: "I don't know that that's actually going to happen". He added, that "if it's through live stream, I'm not going to be watching it". 
Hours later, President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved the live stream plans but the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it. 
Nidal Hasan killed 13 unarmed soldiers at a base in Texas in 2009, injuring another 32. The firing squad execution would be the first military execution in more than 60 years. 
The Pentagon announced earlier this week it would execute Nisan, a former US Army major, on 3 December by firing squad in the attack on the Fort Hood base. 
Then on Thursday US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be livestreamed for the public. "People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth explained. 
Trump, as he left the White House on Friday, was asked about the possibility that visuals of Hasan's execution could be used as propaganda for terrorists. 
"He killed 13, 14 people, badly wounded 20-some-odd people, and he's totally nuts," Trump said. "So I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes, and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him." 
The Pentagon declined to comment further when asked for more information about a decision on the livestream. 
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Vance condemned Hasan's attack on the base as "the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11". Asked about how his Catholic faith impacted his stance on the plan to stream a public execution, Vance questioned whether it would happen. 
But he noted that Hasan, who was a US Army psychiatrist, was meant to treat soldiers for mental illness and other problems and "took them at their most vulnerable and gunned down these people where they lived". 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Trump says he approved the live stream execution of Fort Hood shooter 
The announcement about a possible livestream has been met with criticism from both political parties. 
Republican Senator John Curtis pointed to Rome's history of a "bloody spectacle" corrupting people who watched them, warning that public executions erode civilisations "when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment". 
Curtis said that Hegseth's plan "risks feeding that appetite" and urged him to reconsider. 
"The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent," he said. 
Democratic Senator Chris Murphy told CNN that the idea was "disgusting" and reminiscent of executions carried out by the Islamic State group. 
Georgia lawmaker Austin Scott, a Republican, said that he "absolutely" supports the death sentence, but that live-streaming executions "is what jihadists do. America is better than that". 
John Bolton, a former national security adviser during the first Trump administration, told BBC's Radio 4 PM that he supports capital punishment, but that the livestream is "unnecessary" because there are provisions for interested parties to view the execution in person or to report on it. 
"I just think this is a mark by Secretary Hegseth doing something he thinks will please President Trump. That's the way he's been running the defence department. I think that's really not appropriate for a secretary of defence," Bolton said. 
The US Conference of Catholic Bishops condemned the decision to publicly livestream Hasan's execution, expressing "shock and great sorrow" in a statement. 
The UN human rights office told AFP that livestreaming it would be "tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture". 
Figure caption, 
Can the Fort Hood shooter’s execution be livestreamed? 
Hasan opened fire in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines. 
He later admitted in court that he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military. 
The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base. 
Military law requires that military execution be approved by the US president. It also requires appellate review, when a higher court inspects the decision and gives a final judgement on its legality to move forward. 
While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two nations carried them out publicly. Eleven public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025 and another six in Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International. 
Image source, Getty Images 
- 
Firing squad execution to be livestreamed, Pentagon says 
- Published 6 hours ago 
- 
Fort Hood survivor supports gunman's execution by firing squad but questions livestream 
- Published 15 hours ago 
When Hegseth told reporters on Thursday about plans to ensure the public can watch the execution, he did not specify where or how live video of the execution would be shown. 
A Pentagon spokesperson on Friday reiterated to the BBC that Hasan's execution "will be livestreamed," but said the government had no further details "to provide at this time". 
The White House did not respond to an inquiry about whether it expected to show Hasan's planned execution on its social media channels. 
The White House maintains official accounts and channels on the most notable and widely used online platforms that are capable of streaming live video, namely Meta, YouTube, TikTok and X. 
Figure caption, 
Americans' views on death penalty after failed execution in Tennessee 
All of the platforms have prohibitions in place on violent images and videos, as well as those that show death or glorify or make a spectacle of violence. 
Meta, owner of Instagram, Facebook and Threads, explicitly bans any live stream of capital punishment. 
YouTube bans all "violent or gory content intended to shock or disgust viewers". 
TikTok has a similar rule that bars "extremely graphic, violent, or disturbing content—especially when it could cause viewers emotional distress." That includes the "moment of someone's death" and "the shooting of an individual". 
Both YouTube and TikTok make exceptions in instances of "public interest". 
Asked if a live-stream of an execution qualifies for the exception if it is government-sanctioned , a TikTok spokeswoman said: "Regardless, I'd point you back to the not allowed section which reflects our approach." 
The policy at X, which has loosened content moderation since billionaire Elon Musk took over the platform, prohibits content "glorifying" of violence. It will remove content depicting when a person dies will be removed if requested by certain parties. 
Meta, YouTube and X did not respond to multiple BBC requests for comment on whether they would uphold their current policies in the event Hasan's execution is broadcast.

articles.title: Commentator Katie Zacharia picked as new White House press secretary
articles.summary: The conservative commentator currently works as a communications adviser at Trump Media & Technology Group.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images By Sareen Habeshian   and   Bernd Debusmann ,  White House reporter 
- Published 9 October 2026 
Donald Trump has chosen conservative commentator Katie Zacharia to be the next White House press secretary. 
Zacharia, who currently works for Trump Media & Technology Group, will become the US president's sixth chief spokesperson across his two administrations. She previously had a brief stint as a spokeswoman at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). 
Trump called Zacharia "loyal" and "a devoted fan and member of MAGA" in a social media post on Friday, referring to his Make America Great Again movement, adding that she had "an unblemished record of support". 
Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt, who left the White House in August, has reportedly taken a job with Fox News. 
"She was previously involved in my Campaigns, assisting in key Swing States, where we won 7 out of 7," Trump wrote on Truth Social of Zacharia. 
"I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and my Administration." 
Figure caption, 
Watch: New press secretary is going to be 'terrific', says Trump 
Zacharia thanked him in a post on X, writing: "Serving President Trump and the American people at this critical 250-year mark is the honor of a lifetime." 
She said Trump had "shown America that we can be great again, and he works to effectuate that greatness every single day". 
She said she looked forward "to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out". 
The 42-year-old political strategist is a frequent fixture on conservative Newsmax and Fox News, and has been active in Republican politics for most of her adult life, having worked as an intern for the Republican National Committee and for the White House Office of Political Affairs during the Bush administration in 2006. 
Since June, she has been a senior communications adviser for Trump's media company and Truth Social platform, according to her LinkedIn profile. She worked in Homeland Security from February to March this year. 
While she was only briefly in government at DHS - which the mother of four later said she left because of the strain of travel between California and Washington on her family - she has long been a ferocious defender of President Trump and his administration's policies. 
In a June interview with the BBC , for example, she dismissed criticism of Trump's controversial use of the White House to host a televised UFC fight, saying the principles of the UFC "are the kind of principles that founded our Constitutional Republic". 
"It's about not giving up the fight until the bitter end," she said. "I think there's no better summation of the American ethos than a good UFC fight." 
Earlier this year, Zacharia wrote an op-ed in the New York Post about an incident in which she was asked to stop wearing a "Make America Great Again" hat to her local gym. 
"I responded that I would never take my Trump hat off to appease the left," she wrote. "This is raw, unfiltered intolerance. Freedom of speech doesn't evaporate at the gym door." 
Justin Buchler, a political science professor at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio, told the BBC that Trump's appointments during his second term have been "based on personal affiliation and loyalty". 
"He values loyalty first and foremost," Buchler told the BBC. 
A lawyer educated at Pepperdine University in California, Zacharia also served as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative non-profit started by Trump ally - and current Special Presidential Envoy for Special Missions - Ric Grenell. 
In 2011, she spent nearly two years clerking at a law firm in Beijing, China. 
- 
Trump says White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt to leave post 
- Published 12 August 
The complex job of press secretary goes beyond the briefing room podium to include managing contentious relationships with the press, coordinating with other parts of the White House, and providing media advice to the president. The secretary also oversees an office that receives a significant amount of inquiries and requests on a daily basis. 
Yanna Krupnikov, a political scientist and professor of communication and media at the University of Michigan, said the selection of Zacharia "speaks to a blurring of the lines between different media types". 
Politicians nowadays need to communicate not only to various news outlets but with people in a social media context, she said. 
"I think the goal is not as much speaking to the media and journalists, but making sure that particular, very specific sound-bytes and messages get to ordinary people," Krupnikov told the BBC. 
When Leavitt left the role, Trump called her one of his "most trusted aides", which sets a high bar for her replacement. Leavitt left because she said she wanted to spend more time with her family.

articles.title: 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation
articles.summary: Students taking to the streets in France have become a focal point in the country's increasingly polarised politics.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Hundreds of thousands of students have protested across France since the end of last month By Nick Beake Europe correspondent 
- Published 2 hours ago 
As dustbins burn and students chant "everyone hates the police" in the French city of Lille, one teenager explains why he and his friends have taken to the streets. 
"There aren't even enough chairs. We have to go and find some at the start of every lesson," the 16-year-old, who did not want to give his name, says of his school. 
"We've got 50 minutes to eat at lunchtime but there are 2,000 of us that need to get through the canteen." 
He is one of hundreds of thousands of students who have protested across France since the end of last month over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds. 
Despite the government's apparent attempts to make concessions, the students show no sign of backing down. 
"They have armies, they have the police, they have the powers," says Massicella, 18, as she marches through Lille. "But we have the mass population." 
The protests, which have turned violent, have become a focal point in France's polarised politics, with all sides accusing the other of escalating tensions. As a presidential election approaches, politicians on both the hard right and hard left have sought to capitalise on the unrest and on what many see as the government's inability to resolve the crisis. 
Image caption, 
Massicella, second left, and her friends have been protesting in Lille 
The protests - ignited at the Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in the deprived Paris suburb of Créteil - have struck a chord across the country. 
Videos of rats scuttling through corridors in other lycées soon hit social media, providing striking symbols of the discontent. Other videos on TikTok and Instagram showed broken toilets, holes in walls and mouldy ceilings across the country. Students have complained of unbearable heat in the summer and freezing classrooms in the winter. 
The anger has also focused on long school hours, chronic staff shortages, overcrowded classes and a deeply unpopular university admissions system. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Marseille school students explain why they're protesting 
The problem for the French government - which became clearer as we spoke to dozens of pupils this week - is that even if a tiny minority of schools have a problem with rodents, a very large number of pupils believe their own education is failing them. 
On Tuesday, the government said 250,000 people marched, most of them young. The trade unions said it was more like half a million. 
But it is not just students taking to the streets - their teachers are joining them. 
Secondary school teacher Marine Monins, who joined the demonstrations in Lille, shows us a laminated timetable which she says illustrates the problem. 
It has become normal for pupils to start at 8am and finish as late as 6pm, but the days are punctuated by hours-long gaps because of bad planning and staff shortages. 
When lessons do go ahead, the classes are typically packed with 35 pupils (by comparison, the average secondary school class in England has fewer than 23 pupils). 
"It's now impossible to give every child the attention they deserve," Monins explains. 
Image caption, 
Teachers, including Marine Monins and Marjorie Roussel, have joined their students in calling for change 
On Thursday, the French government made its first sign of ceding ground to protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days. 
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said by the end of October there will be a plan unveiled to respond to the crisis. Ministers have said they could look again at resources for schools within next year's squeezed budget. 
But this has been met with a collective shrug at barricaded school gates across the country. 
"It goes beyond having decent toilets in schools," lycée student Alcidor says in Paris, under the statue of Marianne at Place de la République, a place synonymous with protest. 
"It's strong anger from the youth in France that doesn't feel represented, that feels abandoned, that feels unheard and is scared of what's coming in the future." 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Police have been accused of heavy-handed tactics 
The unrest has resulted in widespread arrests and injuries. 
So far, almost 7,000 people have been detained during the disorder with more than 85% being children, according to the interior ministry. 
More than 700 police officers have been injured in the past three weeks. 
But rights groups and unions accuse the police of resorting to heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flash-ball guns. At least 200 pupils have been injured, along with dozens of teachers. 
A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators in the northern city of Lens. 
Reports of how the teenager sustained the injury differ. A police union source cited by the AFP news agency said the boy appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which then exploded in his hand. However, a witness told local media that the teenager did not pick up the grenade. 
A teacher at the boy's school, Bastien Riez, who is also a union rep, believes that current police tactics could irrevocably damage the relationship with France's youth. 
"For many, this is their first experience of democracy and protest, and they are met with police and a sham of social dialogue and democracy. I fear that many young people will stop believing in this so-called democracy altogether." 
Police have since been banned from using stun grenades at school protests. 
Image caption, 
Kaspar says strangers have been hijacking some protests 
But Parisian pupil Kaspar, 15, speaks of his fear when coming face-to-face with police in full riot gear. He says he and his friends have been protesting peacefully, but strangers were hijacking their protests. 
"These people are coming just to shoot fireworks at police officers and they run. This is not the message we want to send to the world." 
Police chiefs say violence, directed by agitators who have no link to the schools, is making their job incredibly hard. 
Michel Chaballier, deputy secretary-general of the National Police Commissioners' Union (SCPN), says he fears the "political climate has been radicalised", and it was more and more difficult to have a calm, constructive public debate ahead of the national vote next spring. 
"Police officers find themselves caught in the middle of this social tension, which is sometimes fuelled by irresponsible politicians," he says. "That's a shame, because I think this country deserves better." 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Marine Le Pen has condemned damage to schools 
The protests have become another bruising battleground in France's culture wars, with leaders of the hard left and right seeking to capitalise. 
More than three-quarters of under-30s in France interviewed for an Ipsos survey conducted for Aix-Marseille University this week said they were worried about the state of their country. 
But many people have a more profound and wider concern about just how dramatically the middle ground in France is eroding, leaving a chasm in the political landscape. 
The education crisis is symptomatic of this but also threatens to act as an accelerant. 
Most polling suggests more and more French citizens are looking to political extremes for answers to their problems – whether they are linked to education, the economy, identity or immigration. 
Marine Le Pen of the hard right National Rally is the frontrunner in the 2027 presidential race. 
Next, neck and neck, are Édouard Philippe and Jean-Luc Mélenchon. 
Philippe was a prime minister in President Emmanuel Macron's first term and has since founded a centre-right party called Horizons. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Jean-Luc Mélenchon has been supportive of the demonstrations 
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a veteran hard-left politician and founder of France Unbowed (LFI), has been a prominent older face among the students at rallies over the past three weeks. 
Opponents have accused him of provoking and profiting from the unrest, while he counters that only his party truly represents the French youth. 
He claims the current movement that has emerged from the schools protest is the most potent since 1968, when huge demonstrations almost brought down the government of President Charles de Gaulle. At its height, 10 million workers were on the streets before fresh elections led to the revolt fizzling out, but not before carving an indelible memory in French social history. 
Despite being born more than four decades later, an exasperated generation of French teenagers are looking to the past for inspiration. 
"I personally want to reproduce 1968!" Massicella declares in Lille, as she nears the end of the protest march. 
Le Pen has stayed away from the protests and her most notable interventions have come in condemning the damage to schools, which is said to run into the millions of euros. 
She has also suggested that parents of children who have committed the vandalism should pay for repairs. 
The principle of casseur-payeur – those who break have to pay – has been an impassioned topic that has dominated French media this week. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The 1968 protests have carved an indelible memory in French social history 
The problem for President Macron is that there is no quick fix. 
This is not a scenario where there is an unpopular piece of legislation that can be withdrawn in a hasty reverse ferret the prime minister is tasked with performing. That was the case with the gilets jaunes – the relentless protest in high vis jackets over a fuel tax rise nearly a decade ago. 
Wholesale reform of the education system would cost billions – in new classrooms, new facilities, new teachers – and take years to achieve. 
And changes that may seem more easily done – such as a reduction of the length of the school day – would be hugely problematic to implement logistically. 
What is more, any proposals which appease the students and end the current protests would have to be agreed at a time when France's finances are in a mess. 
The cost of servicing the national debt each year has now exceeded the core state education budget. Under the 2027 draft budget, there will be a 1.7% rise in education spending - but this is an under-inflation increase. 
Le Pen has vowed to cut public spending even further if she enters the Élysée Palace. 
She is banking that her promises to cut debt, curb migration and restrict certain benefits to French citizens will eclipse any criticism over her position on the protesting pupils. 
For her, discipline, a traditional curriculum and pride in France's history should be the defining features of every classroom. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Many students have said they will not back down from protesting 
But many students are showing little sign of backing down from another French tradition. 
"In France, we have this tradition and history of revolting," says Alcidor in Paris. 
"That's the way we gained our rights and the way we will always gain them. That's our spirit." 
As the rain came outside the Lycée Voltaire central in Paris this week, the reality of having been up early once again to block the main gate started to kick in and the energy of the crowd dipped. 
But not for long. 
A huge cheer erupted as a senior teacher unlocked the hulking front door and poked her head out into the street. 
"The canteen is still open." 
The hunger for better schools among France's youth and better days for everyone else will not be so easily sated.
